A 33-year-old man with a history of massive small-bowel and ileocecal resection 12 years earlier (leaving 40 cm of small intestine) was maintained on a normal diet after bowel rehabilitation. One month before admission, he developed diarrhea and a 7-kg weight loss with progressive weakness, anorexia, dizziness, and cachexia. On admission his weight was 36 kg (BMI 12.2 kg/m^2), heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 70/50 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 bpm. He was alert and oriented. Physical examination showed pitting edema of the lower extremities, thin skin, a scaphoid abdomen, and no ascites. Chest radiography revealed a dense nodule outside the right upper lung field (thought to be rib calcification). Lower-limb radiographs and renal ultrasonography were normal; gallbladder ultrasonography showed atrophy. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T-wave flattening/inversion in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6, and an incomplete right bundle-branch block. Initial laboratory values included: phosphate 1.10 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.60 mmol/L, calcium 1.7 mmol/L, albumin 27.7 g/L, prealbumin 100 mg/dL, hemoglobin 48 g/L, hematocrit 14.0%, BUN 5.0 mmol/L, and creatinine 86 mg/dL. He was diagnosed with severe malnutrition and received blood transfusion; parenteral nutrition (500 kcal/day); fluids; electrolyte, trace-element, and multivitamin supplementation (including daily thiamine 100 mg IV). Over 24 hours his strength and edema improved. Then he acutely developed profound fatigue and flaccid weakness of all four limbs. His heart rate was 98 bpm, respiratory rate was unchanged, and repeat labs showed a phosphate level of 0.05 mmol/L.

A 70-year-old man with extensive nicotine use and a remote history of laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma (7 years prior) and bladder urothelial carcinoma (10 years prior) underwent dual-chamber pacemaker implantation for sick sinus syndrome 9 months ago. Postoperative checks on days 1, 2, and at 3 months showed normal pacemaker function and a clinically unremarkable pocket. Three weeks before presentation, he tested positive for COVID-19 infection, but his fatigue, dyspnea, and cough persisted and worsened rather than improving. At a routine cardiology visit 9 months after implantation, he reported a new, painless but bothersome swelling over the pacemaker site. On examination, his blood pressure and heart rate were normal, and there were no signs of cardiac decompensation or cachexia. Chest ultrasound revealed a soft tissue mass with increased vascularity surrounding the device. CT imaging confirmed a soft-tissue mass around the pacemaker pocket, and haematoma or infection was excluded.

A 5-month-old dark-skinned boy was seen for evaluation of a congenital skin lesion on the left supraclavicular area. At birth, the lesion measured 11 cm × 3.5 cm; at 5 months it measured 10 cm × 2.5 cm. On examination, it was a single, nonpulsatile, well-demarcated, dark brown atrophic plaque with a linear midline depression and an elevated, compressible, soft border that was paler than the central portion. Birth and neonatal history were unremarkable; the patient was healthy and not on medications. The initial differential diagnosis included smooth muscle hamartoma, semiannular lipoatrophy, and, less likely, a rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma (RICH). A small vein (~0.3 mm) was visible to the naked eye within the plaque. To avoid puncturing larger vessels during a planned biopsy, an AccuVein AV400 infrared vein finder was used; it revealed one large vein with an extensive network of small superficial branching vessels localized to the area of the atrophic plaque. A working diagnosis of probable RICH was made.

clinical_record:
A 65-year-old woman presented with blurry vision in her right eye for several months. Ocular history included 3 recurrent episodes of bilateral iritis occurring during 5 months, amblyopia in the left eye, and bilateral posterior chamber intraocular lens. Patient had undergone left-sided mastectomy 2.5 years prior and had been on anastrozole therapy for more than 2 years. Medical history and past medication use were otherwise unremarkable.

Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/150 OS without improvement on pinhole testing. Intraocular pressures were normal. Right eye showed trace conjunctival injection without definite ciliary flush, 2+ fine keratic precipitates, and 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. Left eye had a few keratic precipitates. Dilated fundus examination revealed cystoid macular edema with a yellow spot in the fovea in the right eye and an epiretinal membrane in the left eye. No inflammation in the periphery was noted in either eye.

Dilated, tortuous veins were noted over the chest and left leg. She had no facial dysmorphism, no cardiac murmur, no organomegaly, full muscle strength, intact reflexes, and normal developmental milestones and growth parameters.

She was born by cesarean delivery to a nonconsanguineous couple; the pregnancy was notable for fetal malformations. Two older siblings were healthy. Skeletal survey demonstrated fused toes (right second and third, left fourth and fifth) with soft-tissue hypertrophy of the involved digits.

clinical_record:
A 54-year-old fisherman with no significant medical history was brought to the emergency department after a rapid ascent from a 50 m sea‐depth saturation dive. He complained of dyspnea, lethargy, severe generalized arthralgia, and mild confusion. He was alert with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 14. Physical examination showed bilateral joint pain worsened by movement without erythema or swelling; neurological, chest, cardiac, and abdominal examinations were otherwise unremarkable. Vital signs were blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, pulse 95 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min, oxygen saturation 90% on room air, and temperature 36.6 °C. The Wells pulmonary embolism score was 3.

High‐flow oxygen was started. An electrocardiogram was normal. Posterior–anterior chest radiography showed no abnormalities. Laboratory tests revealed a white-cell count of 13 × 10^9/L, C-reactive protein 73 mg/L, and otherwise normal hemoglobin, platelets, glucose, ESR, creatinine, urea, potassium, sodium, and D-dimer. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated metabolic acidosis with pH 7.32, PCO2 28 mm Hg, HCO3– 15 mmol/L, and PO2 63 mm Hg. Transthoracic echocardiography showed normal biventricular size and function and no valvular disease; however, spontaneous echo contrast consistent with microbubbles was seen in the right heart chambers. A Valsalva maneuver–enhanced color‐flow Doppler study showed no evidence of a patent foramen ovale.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 24-year-old white man presented with an 8-month history of persistent swelling around his left eye. He had no history of significant acne vulgaris or rosacea and no visual symptoms. He had been evaluated by an allergist and an ophthalmologist and had not improved with corticosteroid ophthalmic solutions or oral antihistamines. On examination, there was non-erythematous, non-pitting edema of the left periorbital region without conjunctival inflammation. Paranasal radiography and maxillofacial CT scans showed only periorbital soft-tissue swelling. Patch testing with the North American Standard Series was negative, and a tuberculin skin test result was negative. A skin biopsy revealed numerous dermal ectatic blood vessels and lymphatics with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate.

clinical_record:
A 35-year-old man presented for routine follow‐up 11 years after a left total hip arthroplasty with a ceramic‐on‐ceramic articulation. Over the preceding 3 months, he had left buttock and greater trochanteric pain, initially attributed to overuse. He denied fevers or systemic symptoms. On examination, range of motion of the left hip was full and painless; there was focal tenderness over the posterior buttock and greater trochanter but no palpable mass. Anteroposterior radiographs of the pelvis and left hip were unchanged compared with images obtained 1 year earlier. A diagnosis of greater trochanteric bursitis was made, and an intra‐bursal corticosteroid injection was administered, resulting in partial symptom relief.

Six weeks later, he returned with persistent buttock pain and intermittent electric shock–like sensations radiating down the left leg. Physical examination now revealed decreased and painful range of motion of the left hip with continued tenderness over the greater trochanter. A lumbar spine radiograph was normal. Laboratory studies showed an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 22 mm/h (reference range, 2–28), a C‐reactive protein level of 14.4 mg/L (reference, <10.0), and an alkaline phosphatase level of 318 IU/L (reference, 40–125). Hip aspiration yielded 10,750 white cells/μL; all cultures were negative. Serum cobalt and chromium levels were within normal limits. A metal artifact reduction sequence MRI revealed a left periprosthetic soft‐tissue mass measuring 9 × 8 × 10 cm, without bony involvement or bone‐marrow edema.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

candidate_registry.label: Adverse Local Tissue Reaction (ALTR) associated with metal-on-metal hip arthroplasty

clinical_record:
A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained. 

Three months later, she had bilateral pneumothoraces requiring a third thoracoscopic intervention. One month after discharge, repeat CT showed resolution of pneumothorax, persistent small air cysts, and faint nodular infiltrates in both lower lobes.

A 36‐year‐old man of Indian origin presented at 2:30 a.m. with acute right‐sided weakness and three episodes of vomiting. He awoke around midnight with headache and vomiting, then noted right‐sided numbness and weakness; there was no visual change or speech disturbance. He had experienced odd sensations and occasional tremors in his right arm and leg over the prior two weeks but had not sought care. His medical history was unremarkable. He was a nonsmoker, denied alcohol or drug use, and worked as a teacher. 

On examination, pulse was 88 bpm, blood pressure 124/87 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He was alert (GCS 15) with intact speech. Findings included partial left ptosis, bilateral torsional nystagmus on vertical and horizontal gaze, equal reactive pupils, and no ophthalmoplegia. Motor strength was 0/5 in the right upper limb, 3/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the right lower limb; left‐sided strength was normal. Reflexes were brisk bilaterally with right ankle clonus; the right plantar response was upgoing. Sensation was intact. NIH Stroke Scale score was 7. Cardiorespiratory examination was normal.

Noncontrast CT of the head showed no acute pathology but revealed an incidental 4 × 6 mm hyperdense focus in the left parasagittal frontal cortex suggestive of a cavernoma. CT angiography demonstrated normal opacification of cervical and intracranial arteries; CT perfusion was symmetric. Admission laboratory studies, including complete blood count, coagulation profile, and kidney, liver, and thyroid function tests, were normal except for a total protein of 87 g/L (normal 60–80). Chest radiograph and 12‐lead ECG were normal. Transthoracic echocardiography with bubble study was unremarkable. HbA1c was 5.4%; lipid profile was within normal limits. 

Brain MRI showed a recent ischemic infarction in the left paramedian medulla without hemorrhagic transformation; the small frontal cavernoma was again noted. MR angiography was unremarkable. A diagnosis of ischemic stroke in a 36‐year‐old gentleman with no apparent risk factors was made, and further investigations were initiated to look for the cause.
